glance: Bangla Hotel at the Hawkers Market in Gaibandha town, the first to sell it, and other restaurants in town
gaibandha-atta-dal.desc: Atta dal is meat, often mutton, cooked into a thick gravy with rice flour or wheat flour. It has been the dish of big meals in Gaibandha's Teesta, Jamuna and Brahmaputra chars for about a century: weddings, large gatherings and the community feast held some weeks after a death. Traditionally it was cooked overnight, served in the morning with plain rice, and eaten off banana leaves. Neighbouring districts know it as pithali, melani or pitli. It has come back into fashion, and town restaurants now sell it.

gaibandha-char-life.desc: Hundreds of thousands of people in Gaibandha live on chars that can appear, grow or vanish within a few years. Families build houses on raised plinths, keep cattle and boats, and move their homes when erosion eats their land. Weekly char markets, boat-borne trade and close-knit communities are part of this river culture. Spending time with char families, ideally with a local guide or organisation, gives a deep sense of Bangladesh's relationship with its rivers.
blocks: How to get there
By boat from Balashi or Phulchhari ghats.
Good to know
Go with a local guide, be respectful when photographing homes, and bring small gifts rather than cash.

glance: 260 km to Gaibandha by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
jamalpur-shahi-mosque-gaibandha.desc: Jamalpur Shahi Mosque stands in Bara Jamalpur village, about 6 km west of Sadullapur upazila town. Local tradition links it with the saint Hazrat Shah Jamal, after whom the union is named, and says it lay buried and overgrown for a long time. In the early 1960s the Gaibandha SDO went looking for it with villagers, and when a storm brought down a huge banyan tree the old mosque came into view. Since then people have called it the Gayebi (mysteriously appeared) Mosque. A veranda was later added in front, a shrine said to be Shah Jamal's sits beside it, and a large pond lies in front.
blocks: How to get there
From Gaibandha take a bus or CNG to Sadullapur, then an auto about 6 km west to Bara Jamalpur.
Good to know
Friday prayers draw big crowds; visit on another day if you want to look around. Dress modestly.

glance: 260 km to Gaibandha by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
naldanga-zamindar-bari.desc: The Naldanga estate in Sadullapur upazila was founded by Kashinath Lahiri, who rose in the 1770s as an accountant and revenue official at the court of Cooch Behar. Among later members of the family was Tulsi Lahiri. Today little survives: two temples, an old well, a large pond and fragments of the boundary wall. The rest has crumbled through neglect. It suits travellers who like piecing together history from traces in the village landscape.
blocks: How to get there
From Gaibandha take a bus or CNG along the Sadullapur–Naldanga road to Naldanga, and ask for the jomidar bari.
Good to know
Go with modest expectations; there is no signage. Respect the temples if worship is going on.

glance: 260 km to Gaibandha by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
fulchhari-chars.desc: Phulchhari upazila is made up largely of chars in the Brahmaputra, reached by country boat from ghats near Gaibandha. In the dry season the islands are covered in fields of maize, chilli, peanuts and lentils, with houses raised on earth plinths against floods. A boat ride shows how families adapt to a river that constantly builds and erodes land. Wide skies and quiet water make it memorable.
blocks: How to get there
Take an auto-rickshaw from Gaibandha town to Phulchhari or Balashi ghat, then hire a boat.
Good to know
Go with a local boatman, carry water and sun protection, and avoid the river in stormy weather.

glance: The Phulchhari chilli haat and markets in Gaibandha town
phulchhari-chilli.desc: The sandy soils of the Brahmaputra chars are ideal for chillies, and Gaibandha's red chillies are known across the country. In the season, farmers bring sacks by boat to the chilli haat in Phulchhari, where green and dried red chillies are piled high. Spread out to dry, they turn the riverbanks and courtyards bright red. Locals use them in bhortas and curries with real heat.
blocks: Good to know
Dried chillies are a practical souvenir; buy whole rather than ground.

glance: 260 km to Gaibandha by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
friendship-centre-gaibandha.desc: The Friendship Centre is a training and community centre built for a development organisation working on the chars. Designed by Bangladeshi architect Marina Tabassum, it is set partly below ground behind an embankment to cope with floods, with brick courtyards, pools and planted roofs. The building won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2016. Architecture lovers come here specially, but it is little known to general travellers.
blocks: How to get there
On the outskirts of Gaibandha town; arrange your visit in advance and take an auto-rickshaw.
Good to know
It is a working facility; contact the organisation ahead to ask about visits or stays.

bardhankuthi.desc: Bardhankuthi in Gobindaganj upazila was the seat of a zamindar family whose estate dominated the area for generations. Brick structures, walls and a temple survive in various states of ruin among trees and ponds. Some local accounts link the site to much older history in the region. It is a quiet place to explore on the way between Bogura and Gaibandha.
blocks: How to get there
Gobindaganj is on the Dhaka–Rangpur highway; take a rickshaw to Bardhankuthi from the town.
Good to know
Watch your step around crumbling walls.

glance: 260 km to Gaibandha by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
balashi-ghat.desc: Just a few kilometres from Gaibandha town, Balashi Ghat is a river port and embankment that has become the town's main outing spot. Green slopes run along the levee, with views across a wide braided river channel dotted with chars. Country boats, horse carts on the sand and fishermen at work make it lively in the dry season. On clear days some people say you can even see distant hills to the east.
blocks: How to get there
About 6 km from Gaibandha town; take an auto-rickshaw or CNG.
Good to know
Go in the late afternoon. Boats can be hired to the chars; agree on the fare first.

gaibandha-rosh-monjori.desc: Rosh monjori is made from small, soft balls of chhana served in rich, thickened sweet milk, a little like rasmalai but with its own character. It is Gaibandha's pride, and visitors are expected to take some home. The recipe is credited to local sweet makers in the town, and Ramesh Sweets is the name most often mentioned. It is best eaten cool and fresh.
blocks: Good to know
It is perishable; keep it cool and eat within a day.

glance: 260 km to Gaibandha by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
raja-birat-mound.desc: In the countryside about 17 km west of Gobindaganj, local tradition places the palace of King Virata, the Mahabharata ruler of the Matsya kingdom. Some structures survived into the 19th century, but by now mostly mounds, bricks and old tanks remain. The Department of Archaeology marked it as a protected site in 1978, and excavations in the Rajahar union area have turned up terracotta plaques, decorated bricks and stone pillar bases. There are plans for wider digging and to open it properly to visitors. For now it is a spot for history enthusiasts.
blocks: How to get there
From Gobindaganj (bus from Gaibandha or Bogura), take an auto west towards Rajahar union and ask for Raja Birater Bari.
Good to know
Don't pick up or remove any bricks or shards; it is a protected site. Wear shoes for walking over fields.
